speaker_role: former admissions officer (former Dartmouth admissions director; author of a college-admissions book)
commercial_incentive: light self-promotion of her own book; otherwise no direct paid service pitch in this video
key_insights: Raw GPA numbers mean little to readers since grading scales vary by school; what matters is the difficulty of coursework and how a student performed within that specific context.
A perfectly polished personal statement paired with sloppy, rushed short-answer responses can be a tip-off that a student received excessive outside editing help.

The clearest signal of a weak application isn't a specific stat threshold but apparent disengagement, such as skipping an alumni interview without explanation or leaving a supplemental question blank.
Supplemental essays are frequently under-invested by applicants relative to the personal statement, yet the speaker says they matter significantly to the committee's decision.

There is no fixed standardized test score cutoff; a strong transcript and recommendations can outweigh a weak test score, but a strong test score paired with a weak transcript looks worse to a reader.
Admissions officers rarely have time to routinely check applicants' social media, but may spot-check specific claims, such as googling a club acronym to verify a stated leadership role.
Course rigor is judged relative to what a given high school actually offers, not against a fixed AP/IB benchmark; a single weak AP exam score does not need to be self-reported at many schools.

No single extracurricular type (sport, club, etc.) guarantees an admissions edge on its own; recruited athletes are evaluated on a separate track, and legacy status is weighed differently school to school.
specific_numbers_or_facts: She read roughly 130 to 160 applications per week during peak review season, per Becky Munsterer Sabky
Regular decision review reportedly began January 1, and early decision review began mid-November, per Sabky
She served as a Dartmouth admissions director for 13 years before leaving the role a couple of years prior to this interview, per Sabky
notable_or_distinctive: Uses a courtroom-lawyer analogy for how an admissions officer builds a case for or against an applicant in committee, and states that admissions officers at different colleges never communicate with each other about specific applicants, calling it a clear ethical line.
reliability_notes: The rapid-fire 73-question format produces brief, generalized answers rather than deeply substantiated claims; the speaker left the role a few years before this interview, so some specifics (policies, test-optional stance) may be dated, and light self-promotion of her own book is present.
